title_original: Ashland Review: A Lovely Touchstone to a Special Corner of America
excerpt_original: Somewhere in Eastern Montana, a small group of people are living lives that appear sealed in amber. Ranchers, horse trainers, bull riders, tribal elders existing in modern times with modern problems, comforted by the simplicities of the past. This is, of course, naive and…

blocks.text: Somewhere in Eastern Montana, a small group of people are living lives that appear sealed in amber. Ranchers, horse trainers, bull riders, tribal elders existing in modern times with modern problems, comforted by the simplicities of the past. This is, of course, naive and belittling to their very real plight, but the feeling is genuine. There is a peace to the natural environment that is captured here. As someone says in the film about living there: “It’s like you can reach up and touch the clouds.”

There is something special about Ashland, the place that lends its name to director Wyatt Maw’s documentary. Filmed over eight years on 16mm, this is a film of beautiful moments. We watch an old cowboy named Swede make his breakfast. We watch a rancher named Mary, who lives with the Amish, do her work while telling us how she’s come to this circumstance. There is a particularly striking shot of a young Amish woman standing in the near frame, while a train blasts past in the far frame.

Maw and Hatti Beanland are responsible for the cinematography, and it is the single most impressive thing in the film. There is also a melodic pace to the edit (by Lance Edmands, Ivete Lucas, and James Carson) that makes the most of each beautiful frame. Despite the brief sub-90-minute running time, there is an appreciated comfortability to the extended length with which scenes of breaking horses and bull riding play out.

They also accent both the dangers and excitement of these kinds of lives. Young Bekah Jo talks through surviving a tragedy while navigating adolescence and eleven siblings. Maw and his team are clearly enamored by their subjects, admiring of this time and place. There is a particularly inviting sequence in which members of the Crow and Northern Cheyenne communities sing and dance, which immediately follows an elder explaining the significance of certain artifacts on rocks nearby.

And while things get a tad repetitive as the film moves along (it sometimes feels as though the same observations are being made once and again), the significance of this sliver of America is undeniable. The site of the Battle of Little Bighorn is only miles away from Ashland, after all. The United States of America may be a young nation, but the land it sits on has memories millennia old. Ashland captures both the past and present in concert with each other, and it’s a joy to observe.
